title: Soft landing and a strong dollar

items.headline: Eating out rebounds in Australia, Canada and the UK as inflation falls to 3%
items.body: Restaurant sales in Australia, Canada and the UK rose about 7% year on year in the second half as inflation dropped from 7% to 3%. Casual-dining and quick-service chains report diners trading back up to full menus after two years of cutting back.

items.headline: Modest dining recovery in France, Germany, Japan, Brazil and South Africa
items.body: Restaurant traffic is up about 3% in France, Germany and Japan and about 4% in Brazil and South Africa. Wage growth has caught up with prices, but households remain more careful than their Anglo-American counterparts.

items.headline: Dollar index jumps 9% to a four-year high
items.body: The Egyptian pound, South African rand, Brazilian real, Indian rupee and Chinese yuan fell 5–12% against the dollar, while the euro, yen, sterling and the Canadian and Australian dollars slipped 3–6%. US companies see overseas profits shrink when converted to dollars. Owners of wholly owned outlets carry the whole loss, franchisors lose only a slice of the royalty, and joint venture partners share it.

items.headline: India scraps its 30% local-sourcing quota for foreign restaurant chains
items.body: The government cut approval time for foreign food-service brands from 18 months to 90 days and removed the 30% quota on locally sourced ingredients. Mall operators in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru are offering prime sites, and 6 in 10 urban households earning above $8,000 a year say they would try a new international brand.

items.headline: Egyptian pound loses a third of its value; inflation hits 31%
items.body: After an IMF-linked float the pound slid from 31 to 48 per dollar within a month, and fuel subsidies were cut by 25%. Imported beef and cooking oil cost about 40% more, and restaurants report 15% fewer visits as families cut back. Chains that own their outlets carry the whole currency loss, while local partners and franchisees absorb part of it.

items.headline: Commodity boom lifts Brazilian wages 6%
items.body: Record soy, iron-ore and oil exports raised real wages about 6% in São Paulo state and the Midwest farm belt. Quick-service and casual-dining traffic is up 8% in cities with large agribusiness employers.

items.headline: Chinese diners return: dining-out spending up 9% in tier-1 cities
items.body: Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen report the strongest weekend restaurant traffic since the slowdown began. Smaller cities remain flat, and households stay cautious about big purchases.

items.headline: European gas prices double; restaurant utility bills up 40% in Germany and the UK
items.body: Wholesale gas doubled to about €90 per MWh after pipeline outages. Utility bills for restaurants rose about 40% in Germany and the UK and 25% in nuclear-heavy France, and Japan pays more for imported LNG. Operators of their own kitchens carry the bill, while franchisors only lose royalties when franchisees cut opening hours.

items.headline: Energy exporters cash in: Alberta, Western Australia and Brazil's oil coast boom
items.body: Oil, gas and coal revenues lift wages about 5% in resource regions such as Alberta, Western Australia and Brazil's offshore-oil coast. Restaurant traffic in Calgary, Perth and Macaé is up 6–10%.

items.headline: South Africa's grid fails: up to 10 hours of power cuts a day
items.body: Stage-6 load-shedding forces restaurants onto diesel generators, raising energy costs about 30% and shortening opening hours. Two rating agencies downgrade the country's outlook, and investors question whether the grid can recover.

items.headline: Container freight rates triple after a key shipping strait closes
items.body: Imported beef, packaging and sauces are scarce. Countries with high import barriers (Brazil, China, Egypt, India, South Africa) have few alternative suppliers and see ingredient costs up about 12%, while Europe, the UK and Japan see about 5% and Canada and Australia about 3%. Franchisors that oblige franchisees to buy from them feel the squeeze more than joint ventures that source locally.

items.headline: China's property slump: home prices fall 12%, household spending drops
items.body: Two large developers default and households feel poorer. Chinese restaurant spending falls about 7% in non-capital cities, and tourist spending in Australia and Japan weakens as Chinese visitors cut back.

items.headline: US–China tariffs reach 40%; Beijing opens food-safety reviews of US restaurant brands
items.body: Beijing retaliated with a 40% tariff on US food imports and ordered audits of US-linked chains. New-outlet permits slowed to a trickle, and wholly owned US brands are the main target. Joint ventures with local partners are being treated more gently.

items.headline: Brazil, Egypt and South Africa demand 50% local sourcing from restaurant chains
items.body: From January, foreign food-service brands must source half of their ingredients locally or pay a 15% levy on imports. Chains that tie franchisees to central US purchasing face the biggest disruption, while those with local partners already buy locally.

items.headline: Buy-local campaigns spread: foreign chains lose younger diners in culturally distant markets
items.body: National food-brand campaigns in China, India, Egypt and Japan push consumers toward domestic names, and foreign chains lose 5–10% of diners under 30 there. Brazil, France and Germany see a smaller 2–4% dip. Brands with a local partner or franchisee look less foreign.

items.headline: Germany enters recession: GDP down 0.8%, unemployment at 6.2%
items.body: Factory orders fall for five months running and job cuts spread to services. France and the UK feel a smaller spill-over through weaker exports.

items.headline: Canada and Australia welcome record immigration: population up 2.5%
items.body: Young arrivals fill city centres in Toronto, Vancouver, Sydney and Melbourne. Restaurant traffic near new housing and campuses is up about 8%.

items.headline: Brazilian real falls 14% as election nears and fiscal worries grow
items.body: Debt worries and populist spending promises send the real sliding, and foreign investors delay projects until after the vote. Import costs rise, and a few foreign chains pause openings.

title: Recoveries, a truce and a wellness shift

items.headline: Sugar, salt and fat levies spread; burger and fried-chicken visits fall
items.body: The UK, Australia and Canada tax high-sugar and ultra-processed menu items and require calorie labels. Visits to burger and fried-chicken chains fall about 8% there, and about 3% in France, Germany, Japan, Brazil and South Africa. Markets with less indulgent habits (China, India, Egypt) barely notice.

items.headline: Egypt steadies: Gulf funds invest $15bn and inflation falls to 14%
items.body: Gulf sovereign funds and an IMF programme rebuild reserves, and the pound has held at 48 per dollar for six months. Restaurant traffic in Cairo and Alexandria is up about 9%, and imported ingredient costs ease.

items.headline: Japan welcomes 45 million visitors as the yen weakens to 165 per dollar
items.body: Relaxed visas and a cheap yen bring record tourism. Restaurants in Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto report visitor-driven sales up about 10%.

items.headline: US–China truce cuts tariffs to 15%; Beijing hands out household spending vouchers
items.body: A partial truce lowers tariffs, and Beijing announces consumption vouchers for lower-income households. US brands report permit approvals resuming, and restaurant traffic in China is up about 6%.

items.headline: European gas prices halve; German factory orders recover
items.body: Storage refills and new LNG terminals bring gas back to €45 per MWh. Restaurant utility bills fall by roughly a fifth in Germany, France and the UK, and German consumers start spending again.

items.headline: UK mortgage resets and French transport and pension strikes squeeze diners
items.body: About 1.5 million UK households face higher mortgage payments, cutting eating-out budgets. In France, a month of strikes disrupts deliveries and lifts wage and logistics costs for restaurants.

title: Slowdown, new rivals and a softer dollar

items.headline: Consumer credit tightens worldwide; restaurant traffic dips about 3%
items.body: Consumer loan rates rise about 2 points and card spending slows in nearly every market. Diners shift from full-service to cheaper quick-service meals.

items.headline: Emerging-market stress: Egypt and South Africa borrowing costs jump 4 points
items.body: Investors pull money from emerging markets. Egypt and South Africa suffer the sharpest outflows and currency weakness, Brazil, India and China see smaller ones, and developed markets are barely affected.

items.headline: Rival US chains announce 300+ openings in Brazil, India, Egypt and South Africa
items.body: Three large American restaurant groups target markets where few competitors exist, and the Chinese, European and Japanese markets receive fewer openings. Rents and staff costs rise in new-entry districts, and incumbents see their share shrink.

items.headline: US rate cuts push the dollar down 7%
items.body: Foreign profits convert into more dollars, and emerging-market currencies recover the most, with the rand, pound and real up 6–9% and developed-market currencies up 3–4%.

items.headline: India's monsoon fails: food prices up 14%
items.body: Rainfall is 20% below normal and vegetable and dairy prices spike, raising ingredient costs. Rural incomes fall and small-town outlets report weaker sales.

items.headline: Housing correction in Australia and Canada: prices fall 11%
items.body: Falling property values and high mortgage costs lead households to cut discretionary spending. Restaurant traffic is down about 6% in Sydney, Melbourne, Toronto and Vancouver.

items.headline: Central banks cut rates: mortgage relief lifts spending in Australia, Canada, the UK and Brazil
items.body: Rates fall 1.5 points in Australia, Canada and the UK and about 3 points in Brazil. Restaurant traffic is up about 7% in the first group, about 5% in France and Germany, and more modestly in South Africa and Japan.

items.headline: Delivery platforms and kitchen automation cut labour costs 8% in high-wage markets
items.body: Smarter scheduling, delivery platforms and kitchen automation reduce staffing hours in Australia, Canada, the UK, France, Germany and Japan. Lower-wage markets see only small gains.

items.headline: South Africa's coalition steadies and power returns
items.body: Private solar and gas projects end load-shedding, and the coalition passes its first full budget. Restaurants cut diesel use, and foreign investors return to Cape Town and Johannesburg.

items.headline: India's urban consumption surges as Western brands become aspirational
items.body: Urban incomes rise about 10% and tariff cuts make sourcing imported ingredients easier. Foreign chains report sales in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru up about 15%.

items.headline: Brazil simplifies consumption taxes and lowers import duties
items.body: A single consumption tax replaces five overlapping ones and import duties on food inputs fall. Restaurant operators in São Paulo and Rio expect operating costs to fall about 4%.

items.headline: Shrinking populations bite in Japan, China and Germany
items.body: Japan and China see falling working-age populations and youth unemployment, and households save more. Restaurants in smaller cities close, and Germany feels a smaller version of the same trend.

items.headline: Egypt's canal revenue falls and fuel prices rise again
items.body: Shipping lines reroute away from the canal, cutting hard-currency earnings by about a fifth, and a new fuel price rise renews cost-of-living pressure. Foreign investors turn cautious again.

items.headline: Drought and wildfires push beef and produce prices up 15% in Australia and Canada
items.body: Herds are culled and crops lost across New South Wales, Queensland, Alberta and British Columbia. Beef and produce prices rise about 15%, squeezing restaurant margins despite good traffic.

items.headline: UK raises employer taxes and minimum wage; restaurant labour costs up 6%
items.body: Higher employer national insurance and a higher minimum wage lift staffing costs. Operators cut hours and raise prices, and franchisors see slower new franchise signings.
